summary.text: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with no known comorbidities presented to the Emergency Department with diarrhea for five days and persistent vomiting for one day after eating undercooked street food. She was conscious, afebrile and hemodynamically stable with a pulse of 110/minute, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and SpO2 98% on room air, and had signs of dehydration. Admission laboratory values in Table 1 were within normal limits except serum tryptase.

After a peripheral intravenous cannula was secured, intravenous ondansetron 4 mg was administered. Within five minutes she became restless with skin flushing, respiratory distress and bronchospasm, her blood pressure dropped to 80/40 mmHg, oxygen saturation fell to 74% and sinus tachycardia at 176/minute was noted. An anaphylactic reaction to ondansetron was suspected.

Resuscitation began with intravenous Ringer’s Lactate and vasopressor support, then intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg. Because hypotension and bronchospasm persisted, an intravenous adrenaline infusion and hydrocortisone were given, and she was intubated under rapid sequence induction. In the ICU, bedside echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 60%, vasopressors were tapered off over six hours and she was extubated uneventfully.

After extubation she was conscious, oriented, afebrile and normotensive. A skin prick test for ondansetron was positive with a 20 mm wheal, and serum tryptase was elevated at 45 µg/L, confirming ondansetron hypersensitivity. The patient survived.
